records.current_summary: South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in South Korea (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: One Wikipedia full-text search round surfaced no dedicated article on trans prisoners in South Korea; the jurisdiction's LGBTQ-rights article documents its only prominent trans-in-state-placement case, military rather than civilian: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; the Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty. The same article records that consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 (up to two years' imprisonment; a gay soldier was sentenced to six months in 2017) and that transgender people are excluded from military service. It contains no information on how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system - no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is described. (Last-resort encyclopedic source; fetched and verified.)

records.current_summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

prison_adds.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
prison_adds.summary: Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

prison_adds.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
prison_adds.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

records.current_summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

prison_adds.title: Prisons luxembourgeoises : Les détenus gays et transgenres sont protégés
prison_adds.summary: L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

records.current_summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

prison_adds.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
prison_adds.summary: Moldovan investigative outlet Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007), who served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca. He says he was held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells — including for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar') — supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the unit for detainees requiring protection) was refused. He describes staff humiliation: forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, opening his bathroom door, and calling him 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' and without any rights being violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. Outcome: de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system with prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

prison_adds.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
prison_adds.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

records.current_summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Mexico section)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section, records only one Mexico-specific policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Mexico.
